newsitem.title: UK: Britain supports report to end child labour in India.
newsitem.headline: Britain supports report to end child labour in India.

text.p: Britain backed a report on Monday urging the country's sports good companies, major players in the Indian export market, to push for better wages and conditions and an end to child labour on the subcontinent.

Clare Short, minister for international development, praised the report by Christian Aid, an agency of British and Irish churches which works with the poor in 60 countries, and said the government would support efforts by British business to promote ethical standards.
"This is an important report. It makes disturbing reading. I fully agree with its analysis and its recommendations," she said in a statement.
"Exploitative child labour is an abuse of human rights. It creates a poverty trap for those children and for their country's future."
The report, entitled "A Sporting Chance", said Indian children as young as seven spend days stitching footballs and boxing and cricket gloves for export to Britain.
It also claimed most of the estimated 30,000 child workers in India are paid a pittance and work long hours in hazardous conditions.
"British companies have unparalleled power to propose a positive solution. Together they account for nearly a third of the Indian sports goods industry's export revenue," the charity said.

"Big companies like Mitre, Umbro and Adidas have the money and the muscle to persuade their existing suppliers to implement codes of conduct pledging basic minimum labour standards, with independent monitoring to ensure compliance."

Rather than ditching their Indian suppliers or imposing a consumer boycott or trade sanctions which would hurt the people it is trying to help, Christian Aid said British business, the new Labour government and international agencies should work together to protect the interests of children and their families in India.

The report detailed the case of 11-year-old Sonia, who stitches Manchester United footballs showing the face and autograph of midfielder Eric Cantona for the equivalent of six pence (10 U.S. cents) an hour.

"The Umbro Copa, a football selling for 14.99 pounds ($24.43)...is stitched by home-based workers earning only two-and-a-quarter percent of that amount, 34 pence (54 cents) per ball," the report said.
Christian Aid wants a similar agreement to the one struck by the Pakistan government, the sports good industry and children's charities to phase out child labour there.
Short said she would make it a priority to discuss the best way to promote child rights with its developing country partners.
